claim: Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) is an emerging pathogen of the order Mononegavirales.
source: Human metapneumovirus (HMPV), an emerging pathogen of this order of viruses (Mononegavirales) is one of the main causes of respiratory tract illness in children.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of HMPV.

claim: HMPV is one of the main causes of respiratory tract illness in children.
source: Human metapneumovirus (HMPV), an emerging pathogen of this order of viruses (Mononegavirales) is one of the main causes of respiratory tract illness in children.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: The C-terminal extension of N plays a role in directly preventing premature uptake of RNA by folding into the RNA-binding cleft.
source: Notably, we observe a role for the C-terminal extension of N in directly preventing premature uptake of RNA by folding into the RNA-binding cleft.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Non-segmented, (-)RNA viruses cause serious human diseases.
source: Non-segmented, (-)RNA viruses cause serious human diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Notable members of Mononegavirales include measles, rabies, Ebola, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and Human metapneumovirus (HMPV).
source: Notable members belonging to this group of viruses (Mononegavirales) include measles, rabies, Ebola, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and Human metapneumovirus (HMPV).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: HMPV is a leading cause of serious respiratory tract infections in children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals.
source: HMPV (Paramyxoviridae, subfamily Pneumovirinae) is a leading cause of serious respiratory tract infections in children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals (Boivin et al., 2003; Osterhaus and Fouchier, 2003; van den Hoogen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In all members of the Mononegavirales, the RNA genome is packaged in the form of a nucleocapsid.
source: In all members of the Mononegavirales, the RNA genome is packaged in the form of a nucleocapsid, a ribonucleoprotein complex consisting of polymerized viral nucleoproteins (N) and RNA (Ruigrok et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The nucleocapsid is a ribonucleoprotein complex consisting of polymerized viral nucleoproteins (N) and RNA.
source: In all members of the Mononegavirales, the RNA genome is packaged in the form of a nucleocapsid, a ribonucleoprotein complex consisting of polymerized viral nucleoproteins (N) and RNA (Ruigrok et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The nucleocapsid protects the viral genome from host nucleases.
source: Besides protecting the viral genome from host nucleases, the nucleocapsid serves as the template for transcription by the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about nucleocapsid function.

claim: The nucleocapsid serves as the template for transcription by the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L.
source: Besides protecting the viral genome from host nucleases, the nucleocapsid serves as the template for transcription by the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about nucleocapsid function.

claim: Nucleocapsid assembly necessitates a pool of monomeric, RNA-free N, termed N0.
source: Nucleocapsid assembly necessitates a pool of monomeric, RNA-free N, termed N0, which is kept in an unassembled state through an interaction with an N-terminal portion of the polymerase cofactor P, until delivered to the sites of viral RNA synthesis (Ruigrok et al., 2011; Curran et al., 1995; Mavrakis et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: N0 is kept in an unassembled state through an interaction with an N-terminal portion of the polymerase cofactor P.
source: Nucleocapsid assembly necessitates a pool of monomeric, RNA-free N, termed N0, which is kept in an unassembled state through an interaction with an N-terminal portion of the polymerase cofactor P, until delivered to the sites of viral RNA synthesis (Ruigrok et al., 2011; Curran et al., 1995; Mavrakis et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The P protein is a multifunctional, modular protein containing large intrinsically disordered regions.
source: The P protein is a multifunctional, modular protein containing large intrinsically disordered regions and is found to be tetrameric in HMPV (Leyrat et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: P is found to be tetrameric in HMPV.
source: The P protein is a multifunctional, modular protein containing large intrinsically disordered regions and is found to be tetrameric in HMPV (Leyrat et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: P binds to the nucleocapsid via its C-terminus.
source: In addition, P binds to the nucleocapsid via its C–terminus, and mediates the attachment of the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about P protein function.

claim: P mediates the attachment of the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L.
source: In addition, P binds to the nucleocapsid via its C–terminus, and mediates the attachment of the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about P protein function.

claim: In pneumoviruses, P recruits the processivity factor M2-1.
source: Furthermore in pneumoviruses, P recruits the processivity factor M2-1 (Leyrat et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Recent crystal structures of P bound to N proteins (N0-P) from vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), Ebola virus, Nipah virus, and measles virus have highlighted P's role in preventing assembly of N by blocking the C-terminal and N-terminal extensions of N.
source: A great deal of effort has been spent on understanding the functions of P and recent crystal structures of P bound to N proteins (N0-P) from vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), Ebola virus, Nipah virus, and measles virus have highlighted its role in preventing assembly of N by blocking the C-terminal and N-terminal extensions of N (CTD-arm and NTD-arm) which facilitate N oligomerization (Leyrat et al., 2011; Guryanov et al., 2015; Leung et al., 2015; Yabukarski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The CTD-arm and NTD-arm facilitate N oligomerization.
source: A great deal of effort has been spent on understanding the functions of P and recent crystal structures of P bound to N proteins (N0-P) from vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), Ebola virus, Nipah virus, and measles virus have highlighted its role in preventing assembly of N by blocking the C-terminal and N-terminal extensions of N (CTD-arm and NTD-arm) which facilitate N oligomerization (Leyrat et al., 2011; Guryanov et al., 2015; Leung et al., 2015; Yabukarski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: N proteins have a strong tendency to irreversibly oligomerize and bind host nucleic acids immediately upon recombinant expression.
source: Biochemical studies of the nucleocapsid building block N are complicated by the fact that N proteins have a strong tendency to irreversibly oligomerize and bind host nucleic acids immediately upon recombinant expression (Gutsche et al., 2015; Tawar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Truncating regions of N that facilitate oligomerization is one technique to mitigate the problem of N oligomerization.
source: One technique to mitigate this problem is to truncate regions of N that facilitate oligomerization (Yabukarski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Fusing the N-terminal domain of P to N is a strategy that has seen success with nucleoproteins from other viruses.
source: To stabilize monomeric full-length N0 we fused the N-terminal domain of P to N, a strategy that has seen success with nucleoproteins from other viruses (Guryanov et al., 2015; Kirchdoerfer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Crystals of RNA-free HMPV N in a monomeric state bound to a P peptide were obtained at 1.9 Å resolution.
source: We obtained crystals of RNA-free HMPV N in a monomeric state and bound to a P peptide at 1.9 Å resolution by adding trace amounts of trypsin (Dong et al., 2007) to prune flexible loops and promote crystallization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results with reference to data in Table 1.

claim: The P peptide is firmly nestled into a hydrophobic surface of the C-terminal domain of N (CTD) primarily composed of α-helices αC1 and αC2.
source: In the structure, the P peptide is firmly nestled into a hydrophobic surface of the C-terminal domain of N (CTD) primarily composed of α-helices αC1 and αC2 (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Ile9, Leu10 and Phe11 of P occupy key positions and insert into the hydrophobic groove of N.
source: Ile9, Leu10 and Phe11 of P occupy key positions and insert into this hydrophobic groove (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The linker connecting N and P in the chimeric construct has been cleaved prior to crystal growth.
source: Unlike the N0-P structure recently reported for measles (Guryanov et al., 2015), we find that the linker connecting N and P in our chimeric construct has been cleaved prior to crystal growth.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and compared to a previous structure.

claim: The P peptide wraps around the CTD and residues 12–28 form an alpha helix that lies atop N.
source: The P peptide wraps around the CTD and residues 12–28 form an alpha helix that lies atop N (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The helix in P is initiated at Gly12 and pinned to the CTD through an aromatic side-to-face interaction of Phe23 with Tyr354 of N.
source: This helix is initiated at Gly12 and pinned to the CTD through an aromatic side-to-face interaction of Phe23 with Tyr354 of N, both residues belonging to the so-called mir motif which is conserved within Pneumovirinae (Karlin and Belshaw, 2012).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and the mir motif is referenced to previous work.

claim: Phe23 and Tyr354 belong to the mir motif which is conserved within Pneumovirinae.
source: This helix is initiated at Gly12 and pinned to the CTD through an aromatic side-to-face interaction of Phe23 with Tyr354 of N, both residues belonging to the so-called mir motif which is conserved within Pneumovirinae (Karlin and Belshaw, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Alanine mutations of the corresponding residues to Phe23 and Tyr354 in respiratory syncytial virus resulted in a drop of polymerase activity by more than 75% in a minireplicon system.
source: This result is consistent with an earlier study, in which alanine mutations of the corresponding residues in respiratory syncytial virus resulted in a drop of polymerase activity by more than 75% in a minireplicon system (Galloux et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Many hydrophobic residues lining the P-binding surface of αC1 through αC2 are shared within the Paramyxoviridae family.
source: Alignment of Paramyxoviridae N sequences revealed that many hydrophobic residues lining the P-binding surface of αC1 through αC2 are shared within the family (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: For all known N0-P complexes, P binds to the CTD of N.
source: For all known N0-P complexes (Leyrat et al., 2011; Leung et al., 2015; Yabukarski et al., 2014), P binds to the CTD of N (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structures and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A sub-region of the CTD is bound by P in all N0-P structures, indicating that it is widely conserved throughout Mononegavirales.
source: Interestingly, although the specific interaction sites diverge (Figure 1D, indicated by white and black arrows), a sub-region of the CTD (Figure 1D, indicated by dotted circle) is bound by P in all structures, indicating that it is widely conserved throughout Mononegavirales.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Assembled HMPV N was purified and crystallized in the form of a decameric N-RNA ring.
source: To this end, we purified and crystallized assembled HMPV N in the form of a decameric N-RNA ring (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results with reference to data in Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Excellent electron density maps at 4.2-Å resolution were obtained by exploiting the ten-fold non-crystallographic symmetry in the rings.
source: By exploiting the ten-fold non-crystallographic symmetry in the rings, we were able to obtain excellent electron density maps at 4.2-Å resolution (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C) and build a reliable model (Karplus and Diederichs, 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results with reference to figures showing electron density.

claim: Assembled HMPV decameric N-RNA rings are ~0.5 MDa in molecular mass.
source: Assembled HMPV decameric N-RNA rings are ~0.5 MDa in molecular mass and 160 Å in diameter and 70 Å in height (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Assembled HMPV decameric N-RNA rings are 160 Å in diameter and 70 Å in height.
source: Assembled HMPV decameric N-RNA rings are ~0.5 MDa in molecular mass and 160 Å in diameter and 70 Å in height (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The observed RNA binding mode in HMPV is similar to that seen in the related RSV N-RNA structure.
source: The observed RNA binding mode is similar to that seen in the related RSV N-RNA structure (Tawar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on comparison with a previously published structure.

claim: The RNA wraps around the N ring and wedges tightly in the cleft between the NTD and CTD of N, which is lined by positively charged residues.
source: The RNA wraps around the N ring and wedges tightly in the cleft between the NTD and CTD of N, which is lined by positively charged residues (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: In members of the Paramyxovirinae, the number of nucleotides in the viral genome is required to be a multiple of six.
source: In members of the Paramyxovirinae, the number of nucleotides in the viral genome is required to be a multiple of six (Calain and Roux, 1993) and the structural basis for this so-called rule of six has been elucidated recently (Gutsche et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The structural basis for the rule of six has been elucidated recently.
source: In members of the Paramyxovirinae, the number of nucleotides in the viral genome is required to be a multiple of six (Calain and Roux, 1993) and the structural basis for this so-called rule of six has been elucidated recently (Gutsche et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In members of the Pneumovirinae, the rule of six is not observed.
source: In members of the Pneumovirinae, however, this rule is not observed (Tawar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Each N subunit in HMPV contacts seven RNA nucleotides.
source: Our structure further highlights this difference; with each N subunit contacting seven RNA nucleotides (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The NTD-arm packs against the flank of the previous protomer in assembled N.
source: The NTD-arm packs against the flank of the previous protomer (Figure 2B, the NTD-arm of Ni+1 packs against Ni).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The CTD-arm latches onto the top of the CTD of the next protomer in assembled N.
source: The CTD-arm in turn latches onto the top of the CTD of the next protomer (Figure 2B, CTD-arm of Ni-1 latches onto CTD of Ni).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The binding site of the P peptide overlaps with the binding sites of the NTD- and CTD-arms.
source: We observed that the binding site of the P peptide overlaps with the binding sites of the NTD- and CTD-arms (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the two crystal structures and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The structures provide conclusive evidence that P hampers subdomain exchange between adjacent proteins in Pneumovirinae.
source: Our structures thus provide conclusive evidence that P hampers subdomain exchange between adjacent proteins in Pneumovirinae.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing overlapping binding sites.

claim: P hampers subdomain exchange between adjacent proteins has been proposed for a range of viruses throughout Mononegavirales.
source: This mechanism has also been proposed for a range of viruses thoughout Mononegavirales (Leyrat et al., 2011; Guryanov et al., 2015; Yabukarski et al., 2014; Alayyoubi et al., 2015) and there is mounting evidence that it may be universal throughout the entire viral order.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There is mounting evidence that the mechanism of P hampering subdomain exchange may be universal throughout the entire Mononegavirales order.
source: This mechanism has also been proposed for a range of viruses thoughout Mononegavirales (Leyrat et al., 2011; Guryanov et al., 2015; Yabukarski et al., 2014; Alayyoubi et al., 2015) and there is mounting evidence that it may be universal throughout the entire viral order.
evidence: This is based on inference from multiple cited studies.

claim: A hinge-like motion has been proposed by which N alternates between an open, RNA-free conformation (N0) and a closed RNA-bound (N-RNA) conformation.
source: A hinge-like motion has been proposed by which N alternates between an open, RNA-free conformation (N0) and a closed RNA-bound (N-RNA) conformation (Guryanov et al., 2015; Yabukarski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Comparison of N-RNA and N0-P states for HMPV reveals a rigid body movement of the NTD relative to the CTD.
source: Comparison of these two states for HMPV reveals a rigid body movement of the NTD relative to the CTD (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the two crystal structures and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The conformational change rotates the NTD towards the CTD by 10°.
source: The conformational change rotates the NTD towards the CTD by 10°, the interface between the two domains acting as a hinge.
evidence: This is measured from the crystal structures.

claim: At the interface, hinge residues Thr257 and Ala254 play a particularly crucial role.
source: At the interface, hinge residues Thr257 and Ala254 play a particularly crucial role.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis.

claim: In the open, RNA-free state the hinge is maintained in a helical conformation by stabilization of Ala254 through the side chain of Thr257 and an additional backbone interaction with Thr175.
source: In the open, RNA-free state the hinge is maintained in a helical conformation by stabilization of Ala254 through the side chain of Thr257 and an additional backbone interaction with Thr175 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Upon RNA binding, Thr257 contacts the backbone of a nucleotide instead of stabilizing Ala254.
source: Upon RNA binding, Thr257 contacts the backbone of a nucleotide instead of stabilizing Ala254 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The loop containing Thr157 retracts to sterically accommodate the RNA chain upon RNA binding.
source: In addition, the loop containing Thr157 retracts to sterically accommodate the RNA chain.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Having lost the stabilizing contacts of Thr257 and Thr157, the helical hinge region around Ala254 unravels and becomes flexible.
source: Having lost the stabilizing contacts of Thr257 and Thr157, the helical hinge region around Ala254 unravels and becomes flexible (Figure 2F, indicated by white arrow), allowing the relative domain motions of NTD and CTD.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Tyr252 is important in facilitating the hinge motion.
source: Furthermore, we propose that Tyr252 is important in facilitating the hinge motion.
evidence: This is proposed based on structural analysis.

claim: Tyr252 is positioned just before the pivot point and packs tightly against αC3.
source: Tyr252 is positioned just before the pivot point and packs tightly against αC3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: An aromatic residue at the position of Tyr252 is found packing against the same helix in most known structures of N.
source: An aromatic residue at this position is found packing against the same helix in most known structures of N (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B–G).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B–G.

claim: Transition from the RNA-free to RNA-bound state induces a rotation of αC3, exerting upwards pressure on Tyr252 that is conferred onto the NTD.
source: Transition from the RNA-free to RNA-bound state induces a rotation of αC3, exerting upwards pressure on Tyr252 that is conferred onto the NTD (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: In structures of Paramyxovirinae N, which obey the rule-of-six, the aromatic residue at the position of Tyr252 is flipped in the opposite direction.
source: Intriguingly, in structures of Paramyxovirinae N, which obey the rule-of-six, this aromatic is flipped in the opposite direction (Figure 2—figure supplement 4H,I) and contacts RNA (Gutsche et al., 2015), suggesting a similar coupling of RNA-binding and hinge-motion in these viruses.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4H,I and cited work.

claim: The aromatic residue in Paramyxovirinae N contacts RNA.
source: Intriguingly, in structures of Paramyxovirinae N, which obey the rule-of-six, this aromatic is flipped in the opposite direction (Figure 2—figure supplement 4H,I) and contacts RNA (Gutsche et al., 2015), suggesting a similar coupling of RNA-binding and hinge-motion in these viruses.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The observation of the aromatic residue contacting RNA in Paramyxovirinae suggests a similar coupling of RNA-binding and hinge-motion in these viruses.
source: Intriguingly, in structures of Paramyxovirinae N, which obey the rule-of-six, this aromatic is flipped in the opposite direction (Figure 2—figure supplement 4H,I) and contacts RNA (Gutsche et al., 2015), suggesting a similar coupling of RNA-binding and hinge-motion in these viruses.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison and cited work.

claim: In the polymeric, RNA-bound state of N (N-RNA) the CTD-arm flips upwards and latches onto the next protomer.
source: In the polymeric, RNA-bound state of N (N-RNA) the CTD-arm flips upwards and latches onto the next protomer, whilst in the monomeric state (N0) it packs down against the core of N (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the monomeric state (N0) the CTD-arm packs down against the core of N.
source: In the polymeric, RNA-bound state of N (N-RNA) the CTD-arm flips upwards and latches onto the next protomer, whilst in the monomeric state (N0) it packs down against the core of N (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The downward, monomeric conformation of the CTD-arm is stabilized by specific salt-bridges linking the CTD-arm with the core of N.
source: The downward, monomeric conformation is stabilized by specific salt-bridges linking the CTD-arm with the core of N (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the downward position, the negatively charged CTD-arm folds into the positively charged RNA binding cleft, occupying it and directly blocking the binding of RNA.
source: In this position the negatively charged CTD-arm folds into the positively charged RNA binding cleft, occupying it and directly blocking the binding of RNA (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In VSV, the P peptide inserts itself into the RNA binding cleft.
source: It is interesting to note, that whilst the CTD-arm blocks the RNA site in HMPV, it is the P peptide that inserts itself there in VSV (Leyrat et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The P peptide inserting into the RNA binding cleft is not observed in paramyxoviral N0-P complexes.
source: Because this is not observed in paramyxoviral N0-P complexes (Guryanov et al., 2015; Yabukarski et al., 2014) we hypothesize that, in Rhabdoviridae, a different strategy has evolved to block off the RNA binding cleft.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In Rhabdoviridae, a different strategy has evolved to block off the RNA binding cleft.
source: Because this is not observed in paramyxoviral N0-P complexes (Guryanov et al., 2015; Yabukarski et al., 2014) we hypothesize that, in Rhabdoviridae, a different strategy has evolved to block off the RNA binding cleft.
evidence: This is hypothesized based on structural comparison.

claim: In the RNA-free state, Arg260 and Trp261 contact Glu375, while Arg186 forms a salt-bridge with Asp373 of the CTD-arm.
source: In the RNA-free state, Arg260 and Trp261 contact Glu375, while Arg186 forms a salt-bridge with Asp373 of the CTD-arm (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the assembled, RNA-bound state, Arg186 and Trp261 position RNA nucleotides in the cleft, whilst Arg260 fastens onto the NTD-arm of the neighbouring Ni+1.
source: In the assembled, RNA-bound state these interactions are broken, with Arg186 and Trp261 now positioning RNA nucleotides in the cleft, whilst Arg260 instead fastens onto the NTD-arm of the neighbouring Ni+1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The shift from initial stabilization of the inhibitory (downwards) CTD-arm conformation to stabilization of bound RNA and neighbouring N subunit implies that attachment of a new N protomer and insertion of nascent RNA occur concomitantly.
source: The shift from initial stabilization of the inhibitory (downwards) CTD-arm conformation to stabilization of bound RNA and neighbouring N subunit implies that attachment of a new N protomer and insertion of nascent RNA occur concomitantly.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data.

claim: A semi-conserved LGLT-motif is found within the CTD-arms of Paramyxoviridae.
source: We find a semi-conserved LGLT-motif within the CTD-arms which is followed by a stretch of residues with helical propensity.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The LGLT-motif is followed by a stretch of residues with helical propensity.
source: We find a semi-conserved LGLT-motif within the CTD-arms which is followed by a stretch of residues with helical propensity.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The beginning of the helical stretch preferentially features negatively charged residues at positions equivalent to HMPV which may pack against the complementary charges of the RNA binding cleft.
source: The beginning of this stretch preferentially features negatively charged residues at positions equivalent to HMPV which may in turn pack against the complementary charges of the RNA binding cleft.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence alignment and structural analysis.

claim: Analysis of structures of more distantly related members of Mononegavirales shows that negatively charged residues in the CTD-arm are topologically conserved.
source: Indeed, analysis of structures of more distantly related members of Mononegavirales shows that these negatively charged residues are topologically conserved and that a switch to the downward conformation would position these residues into the RNA binding cleft (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A switch to the downward conformation would position negatively charged residues of the CTD-arm into the RNA binding cleft in distantly related Mononegavirales.
source: Indeed, analysis of structures of more distantly related members of Mononegavirales shows that these negatively charged residues are topologically conserved and that a switch to the downward conformation would position these residues into the RNA binding cleft (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reported structures provide a molecular level rationale for how nucleocapsid assembly is controlled through P by sterically blocking the binding sites of the NTD- and CTD-arms.
source: In conclusion, the reported structures of a paramyxoviral N protein reveal two distinct conformational states, N bound either to the polymerase cofactor P or to RNA. A direct comparison of these two structures provides a molecular level rationale for how nucleocapsid assembly is controlled through P by sterically blocking the binding sites of the NTD- and CTD-arms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural data presented.

claim: This work elucidates a key role of the CTD-arm in hindering premature RNA insertion into the binding cleft.
source: In addition, this work elucidates a key role of the CTD-arm in hindering premature RNA insertion into the binding cleft, thus presenting a mechanistic explanation of how premature RNA uptake is directly inhibited in Paramyxoviridae.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural data presented.

claim: Peptides of the N0-binding region of P have previously been shown to inhibit replication activity in RSV.
source: Peptides of the N0-binding region of P have previously been shown to inhibit replication activity in RSV (Galloux et al., 2015), Nipah virus (Yabukarski et al., 2014), and rabies virus (Castel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Peptides of the N0-binding region of P have previously been shown to inhibit replication activity in Nipah virus.
source: Peptides of the N0-binding region of P have previously been shown to inhibit replication activity in RSV (Galloux et al., 2015), Nipah virus (Yabukarski et al., 2014), and rabies virus (Castel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Peptides of the N0-binding region of P have previously been shown to inhibit replication activity in rabies virus.
source: Peptides of the N0-binding region of P have previously been shown to inhibit replication activity in RSV (Galloux et al., 2015), Nipah virus (Yabukarski et al., 2014), and rabies virus (Castel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The characterization of P-binding surfaces on N proteins is of biomedical importance as these surfaces constitute genuine targets for the development of antivirals.
source: The characterization of P-binding surfaces on N proteins is therefore of biomedical importance as these surfaces constitute genuine targets for the development of antivirals.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous statement about peptides inhibiting replication.

claim: The full-length N gene from human metapneumovirus (strain NL1-00, A1) was cloned into the pOPINE expression vector.
source: The full-length N gene from human metapneumovirus (strain NL1-00, A1) was cloned into the pOPINE expression vector, which includes a C-terminal His-tag, using the In-Fusion system (Takara Clontech, Mountain View, CA) following standard procedures.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: The pOPINE expression vector includes a C-terminal His-tag.
source: The full-length N gene from human metapneumovirus (strain NL1-00, A1) was cloned into the pOPINE expression vector, which includes a C-terminal His-tag, using the In-Fusion system (Takara Clontech, Mountain View, CA) following standard procedures.
evidence: This is stated as part of the experimental methods.

claim: The N0-P hybrid gene was generated by fusing the sequence corresponding to the first 40 residues of HMPV P to the 3' end of the full-length N gene.
source: The N0-P hybrid gene was generated by fusing the sequence corresponding to the first 40 residues of HMPV P (strain NL1-00, A1) to the 3' end of the full-length N gene using overlapping primer PCR.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: A diamond-like, diffraction quality N-RNA crystal was obtained after 132 days.
source: A diamond-like, diffraction quality N-RNA crystal was obtained after 132 days in mother liquor containing 100 mM Tris/Bicine, pH 8.5, 90 mM NPS (NaN03, Na2HPO4, (NH4)2SO4), 37.5% methyl-2 4-pentanediol, polyethylene glycol 1000 and polyethylene glycol 3350 of the MORPHEUS crystal screen.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results.

claim: N0-P crystals were obtained via in-situ proteolysis using 1 µg of trypsin per 1000 µg of sample.
source: For the N0-P hybrid, crystals were obtained via in-situ proteolysis (Dong et al., 2007) using 1 µg of trypsin per 1000 µg of sample.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: The structure of N0-P was solved by molecular replacement using PHASER with the structure of RSV N as a search model.
source: The structure of N0-P was solved by molecular replacement using PHASER (McCoy et al., 2007) with the structure of RSV N (Tawar et al., 2009) as a search model.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: The HMPV N model starts at residue 30 and ends at residue 383 of the total 394.
source: Iterative rounds of refinement using PHENIX (Adams et al., 2010) with TLS parameters and manual building in COOT (Emsley and Cowtan, 2004) resulted in a model for HMPV N starting at residue 30 and ending at residue 383 of the total 394.
evidence: This is a direct report of the model built from the crystal structure.

claim: Residues 101 to 111 of HMPV N were found to be disordered and were not included in the model.
source: Residues 101 to 111 were found to be disordered and were not included in the model.
evidence: This is a direct report of the model built from the crystal structure.

claim: Of the 40 P residues contained in the N0-P construct, the first 28 were well-resolved.
source: Of the 40 P residues contained in our N0-P construct the first 28 were well-resolved.
evidence: This is a direct report of the model built from the crystal structure.

claim: The structure of the RNA-bound subnucleocapsid ring was solved with PHASER using a decameric model of the high-resolution HMPV N structure as a search model.
source: The structure of the RNA-bound subnucleocapsid ring was solved with PHASER (McCoy et al., 2007) using a decameric model of our high-resolution HMPV N structure as a search model.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: Purified N-RNA preparations were analyzed via electron cryomicroscopy (cryo-EM).
source: N-RNA rings were analysed via electron cryomicroscopy (cryo-EM).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: Upon delivery of fresh N0-P to the growth site, addition of the next N protomer (Ni+1) to the filament necessitates that the CTD-arm of the terminal Ni unbinds and flips upwards.
source: Upon delivery of fresh N0-P to the growth site, addition of the next N protomer (Ni+1) to the filament necessitates that the CTD-arm of the terminal Ni unbinds and flips upwards (Figure 3D, indicated by dotted arrow), latching onto Ni+1 and displacing P.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the structural data and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the proposed model, the CTD-arm switching to the upward conformation is driven by the formation of new interactions to the NTD- and CTD arms and the concerted insertion of nascent RNA into the RNA binding cleft of Ni.
source: In our model, this is driven by the formation of new interactions to the NTD- and CTD arms and, importantly, the concerted insertion of nascent RNA into the RNA binding cleft of Ni, with the CTD-arm switching into the upward conformation.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the structural data.

claim: The growth of the nucleocapsid filament is reminiscent of a zipper closing up with one row of teeth corresponding to nascent viral RNA and the other to newly delivered N subunits which interdigitate in a fluid, concerted motion.
source: In this model the growth of the filament is reminiscent of a zipper closing up with one row of teeth corresponding to nascent viral RNA and the other to newly delivered N subunits which interdigitate in a fluid, concerted motion.
evidence: This is an analogy used to describe the proposed model.
